planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a chunky, fast-draining epiphyte mix; give a moss pole or trellis, since vigorous stems climb readily once established.

directions: Pot this southern-China native in a chunky bark-and-perlite epiphyte mix and let the top layer dry before rewatering, since the broad, bold leaves hold moisture reserves and resent sitting wet. Each leaf carries a dense, downy fuzz that gives the whole vine a soft, velvety texture distinct from the glossy-leaved Hoya species already common in cultivation. Bright, indirect light coaxes mature plants into producing large, rounded umbels of fragrant, star-shaped flowers, so provide a trellis or moss pole and resist the urge to prune off the short woody spurs that reflower season after season. Keep humidity on the higher side to prevent the fuzzy foliage from crisping at the edges indoors.

planting.note: Grow in a small hanging pot of well-draining, organic-rich epiphyte mix in bright but diffused light; shield strictly from direct midday sun, which scorches the tiny succulent leaves.

directions: Hailing from cool, misty mountain forests in Vietnam, this miniature wax vine covers its slender, twining stems in tiny, fleshy leaves that look like scattered grains of rice, making it a popular choice for small hanging pots and mixed Hoya collections. Place in bright, diffused light rather than direct sun, which quickly burns the small leaves, and let the top third of the mix dry before watering again. A modest night-time temperature drop and slightly elevated humidity help the dense, trailing growth stay compact and encourage clusters of small, fragrant flowers. Avoid heavy, water-retentive soil, which invites root rot in this fine-rooted species.

planting.note: Grow in bright, indirect to filtered light in a chunky, well-draining mix; this species naturally grows pressed against shaded limestone rock faces, so it tolerates lower light than many Hoya.

directions: Native to limestone outcrops and deeply shaded rock faces across southern China, Laos, and Vietnam, this lithophytic wax vine tolerates lower indoor light levels better than most glossy-leaved Hoya species. Thick, dark green, oval leaves carry a soft fuzz and flush reddish along the margins under brighter light, while clusters of small, fragrant white-to-pale-pink star-shaped flowers appear once the vine matures. Let the chunky mix dry slightly between waterings and check the fuzzy foliage regularly, since the fine hairs tend to trap pests more readily than smooth Hoya leaves. Cooler winter temperatures are tolerated better than in many tropical Hoya relatives.

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket of fast-draining, chunky epiphyte mix in bright, indirect light; the trailing habit suits a shaded shelf or basket better than a climbing trellis.

directions: This Philippine species favors a trailing rather than climbing habit, making it well suited to a hanging basket of chunky, fast-draining mix in a shaded corner. Thick, succulent, ovate leaves stay green in filtered light but develop maroon-red margins under brighter conditions, and clusters of small yellow flowers form once the vine is established. Allow the mix to nearly dry out between waterings, since the waxy leaves store moisture and are prone to rot in soggy soil. Keep humidity on the higher side and avoid direct midday sun, which can scorch the foliage.

planting.note: Grow in bright, filtered light in a chunky bark-and-perlite mix with a trellis for the thin, twining stems; morning sun deepens leaf color but harsh midday sun scorches the foliage.

directions: Known among collectors as the claw hoya for its dramatic, deep maroon, claw-shaped flowers, this species pairs narrow, firmly textured, prominently veined leaves with slender, flexible vining stems. Provide several hours of bright, filtered light to encourage blooming, since harsh direct midday sun scorches the thick leaves while too little light produces a leggy, flower-shy vine. Let the top few inches of a chunky, well-draining mix dry before watering again, as the fleshy leaves tolerate underwatering far better than soggy roots. Give a trellis or wire hoop for support and repot only occasionally, since this species flowers best when slightly pot-bound.

planting.note: Grow in bright, indirect light to light partial shade in a well-draining epiphyte mix with a trellis; this fast-growing, easy-care species tolerates average home conditions better than many Hoya.

directions: Native to the Philippine Islands, this twining wax vine takes its name from the faintly camphor-like scent released when its leaves are crushed or bruised. It grows and flowers quickly compared with many slower Hoya species, producing small, pretty pink star-shaped flower clusters even on relatively young plants, which makes it a good candidate for beginners moving beyond the common Hoya carnosa. Water once the soil surface has dried, keep the mix well-drained to avoid the clogged, soggy conditions this species dislikes, and provide a trellis or hoop for the vigorous, twining stems. Protect from temperatures below 50 degrees Fahrenheit, since cold quickly damages the foliage.

planting.note: Grow in bright, indirect light in a well-draining, organic-rich mix with support for the twining stems; water well in active growth and let the mix dry out more in winter.

directions: This Indonesian species earns its name from leaves that vary noticeably in shape and succulence from plant to plant, with lowland, beach-growing forms typically producing thicker, more succulent foliage able to handle brighter light than typical shaded houseplant conditions. It begins flowering relatively early in its development and continues steadily through the warm growing season, bearing fragrant clusters of waxy flowers on short, reusable spurs that should not be removed when tidying the vine. Give bright, indirect light and a well-draining, organic-rich mix, watering thoroughly in summer and allowing the mix to dry out more between waterings over winter. Protect from temperatures below 50 degrees Fahrenheit year-round.
